title: Meta Shelves Class C Stock Issuance to Preserve Zuckerberg's Control as Shareholder Lawsuit Looms
text:
Meta Shelves Class C Stock Issuance to Preserve Zuckerberg's Control as Shareholder Lawsuit Looms — BigGo Finance Ask AI News Markets Earnings Calls Calendar Watchlist Podcasts Influencers Earnings Calls Calendar Watchlist Podcasts Influencers More Ask AI News Watchlist Holdings Markets Earnings Calls Calendar Podcasts Influencers Meta Shelves Class C Stock Issuance to Preserve Zuckerberg's Control as Shareholder Lawsuit Looms
 Add preferred source Meta Platforms has decided to hold off on issuing non-voting Class C stock until litigation brought by shareholders is resolved. The company had planned to introduce the new share class as a stock dividend in January next year, a move that would have let CEO Mark Zuckerberg cash out part of his stake while retaining roughly 61% of voting power. But shareholders including CalSTRS and Denmark's PFA sued in the Delaware Court of Chancery, alleging the board breached its fiduciary duties, and 10 suits have been consolidated ahead of an April trial. Meta says it may need hundreds of billions of dollars over several years to fund AI infrastructure, and that the new share class would broaden its financing options. Key Elements 
 Meta Platforms Mark Zuckerberg Delaware Court of Chancery California State Teachers' Retirement System (CalSTRS) PFA Class C stock Class B stock Kathaleen St. J. McCormick artificial intelligence (AI) investment Meta Platforms has decided to halt a planned issuance of a new class of stock — designed to raise capital for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investment while preserving CEO Mark Zuckerberg's grip on the company — until its legal dispute is resolved. The move follows a lawsuit in which shareholders allege the board breached its fiduciary duties.
 In a filing with a Delaware court on the 18th (local time), Meta said it will not issue non-voting Class C stock while the litigation is pending. The company had originally planned to create the Class C shares on January 19 next year and distribute them to existing shareholders as a stock dividend. Had the plan gone through, Zuckerberg would have been able to cash out part of his holdings while retaining roughly 61% of the voting power.
 "For the best interests of our shareholders, we intend to obtain a final ruling as expeditiously as the court will allow," Meta said in a statement, adding that it will "vigorously defend against the claims raised in the litigation." A trial is scheduled for April next year.
 At the heart of the dispute is whether the board acted independently and whether the non-voting stock unfairly harms ordinary shareholders. Plaintiffs include the California State Teachers' Retirement System (CalSTRS) and Danish pension group PFA, and the 10 lawsuits have now been consolidated into one.
 Lawyers for the plaintiffs argued that "ordinary shareholders receive a stock dividend proportional to their holdings but are not given corresponding governance protections or a vote on the transaction." They added that "shareholders bear the economic costs and market burden created by the non-voting stock while still being unable to exert influence over the company's major decisions."
 Meta maintains that the board's approval followed a unanimous recommendation from a special committee composed of disinterested independent directors, and that the plan serves the interests of both the company and shareholders. The company has sought an expedited trial to quickly resolve the legal uncertainty, but the plaintiffs are asking Delaware Court of Chancery Chancellor Kathaleen St. J. McCormick for a longer trial schedule.
 Behind Meta's push to restructure its share structure is the AI race. In court filings, the company said the new share class would broaden its financing options and allow it to invest in growth across its AI-driven businesses. According to internal projections cited in court documents, Meta may need to raise hundreds of billions of dollars over the coming years to support its AI ambitions.
 The plan emerged from a capital-structure review that began in late 2025. The company sought a way to secure investment funding while preserving incentives for Zuckerberg, and the result was a proposal to distribute non-voting Class C stock to existing shareholders at a 2-to-1 ratio. Zuckerberg currently holds about 61% of the company's voting power, primarily through Class B shares that carry voting rights.
 This is not the first time Meta has attempted a special voting structure. The company pursued a similar plan in 2017 but withdrew it ahead of testimony in a lawsuit brought by minority shareholders in a Delaware court. At the time, investors objected that the arrangement would create a gap between Zuckerberg's voting power and his economic stake.
 The current lawsuit comes as Meta must simultaneously tackle two challenges: expanding AI investment and raising capital. As more companies find it difficult to access the bond market, the need to raise funds through equity issuance is growing, but governance controversies can weigh on investor sentiment. Wall Street observers say the outcome of the trial could alter the course of Meta's financing plans and shareholder return policy.
 Category Details 
 Planned stock Non-voting Class C stock (via stock dividend) 
 Original issuance date January 19, 2027 
 Zuckerberg's voting stake About 61% (mainly Class B shares) 
 Consolidated lawsuits 10 
 Trial scheduled April 2027, Delaware Court of Chancery 
 Key plaintiffs California State Teachers' Retirement System (CalSTRS), Denmark's PFA 
 Note: Issuance date and trial schedule are based on local media reports.
 Meta has decided not to issue Class C stock until the trial concludes, but it maintains its position of seeking a ruling as quickly as the court allows. Investors are increasingly focused on the possibility that a prolonged legal battle could limit the company's options for raising capital to fund AI investment.
